notes.b: Obesity develops when the energy taken in as food regularly exceeds the energy the body uses, and the surplus is stored as fat (adipose tissue).
points: Body mass index (BMI) is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. A BMI of 30 or more in adults is classed as obese, and 25 to under 30 as overweight.
Fatty and sugary foods are energy-dense, which means a small portion supplies a large amount of energy, so it is easy to take in more than the body needs.
Sugary drinks, cream sauces, fried foods, large portions, snacking, late-night eating, too much processed food and a low-fibre diet all increase energy intake.
Not all causes are dietary. Inactivity, heredity, stress and emotional eating also contribute, and a sedentary lifestyle means less energy is used up.
Obesity increases the risk of coronary heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and gallstones, as well as joint strain and arthritis, breathing problems and low self-esteem.
Weight-loss guidance is a balanced low-energy diet: lower fat (especially saturated fat), reduced sugar and salt, extra fibre, fruit, vegetables and water, lean protein and less processed food.

Low-fat cooking methods, removing visible fat from meat, avoiding cream sauces, smaller portions, avoiding alcohol and late-night eating, and regular exercise all help, because they cut energy in and raise energy used.
notes.tip: If asked for three lifestyle changes or guidelines for an obese person, give clear actions such as a lower-fat, lower-sugar diet, smaller portions and regular exercise, and say why each one reduces energy balance. Obesity from excess calories is also a safe answer when asked to name a diet-related condition and a cause.

notes.b: Coronary heart disease (CHD) happens when the coronary arteries, which supply the heart muscle with blood, become narrowed or blocked by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis), which can cause angina or a heart attack.
points: Saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol, which is deposited in artery walls and narrows them, so less blood reaches the heart muscle.
Trans fats, found in some hard margarines and in fried and processed foods, raise LDL and lower HDL cholesterol, so they are doubly harmful.
Refined carbohydrates and sugar contribute to raised blood triglycerides (blood fats), reduced HDL cholesterol and weight gain.
Excess salt raises blood pressure, which damages artery walls and makes the heart work harder.
A diet low in fibre, fruit and vegetables offers little protection against CHD, because these foods help lower blood cholesterol.
Other causes are smoking, lack of exercise, obesity, excess alcohol, stress, high blood pressure, heredity, age and gender.

Cholesterol is a soft, wax-like substance found in every body cell. The liver makes most of it, with some coming from animal foods. It forms part of cell membranes and bile, is needed to make some hormones, and helps transport fats in the blood.

LDL cholesterol (associated with saturated fat) deposits cholesterol in artery walls, hardening and narrowing them. HDL cholesterol (associated with unsaturated fat) carries cholesterol away from the arteries to the liver.
notes.tip: A question asking for three causes of CHD wants specific causes, each linked to the heart or arteries, such as saturated fat, excess salt, smoking or lack of exercise. For an account of cholesterol, include what it is, what it does in the body, and the difference between LDL and HDL. Saturated fat is the usual example of a diet cause.

notes.b: Diabetes means the level of glucose in the blood is raised. It happens because of a problem with insulin, a hormone made by the pancreas that lets glucose move from the blood into body cells.
points: Type 1 diabetes (insulin-dependent): the pancreas produces little or no insulin. It often starts in childhood, adolescence or young adulthood, may be hereditary, is controlled with insulin, diet and exercise, and cannot be reversed.

Type 2 diabetes (non-insulin-dependent): insulin is produced but cells respond poorly to it, or too little is made. It usually develops later in life, although some young people now develop it, and it accounts for about 90 per cent of cases.
Excess weight and inactivity are the main risk factors for Type 2 diabetes. Diets high in sugar and refined carbohydrate, combined with excess weight, raise the risk. Sugar alone is not the cause.
Type 2 can often be controlled with diet, weight loss, exercise and tablets, so losing weight can improve it.
Gestational diabetes develops during pregnancy and usually resolves after the birth.
Symptoms include frequent urination, thirst, hunger, weight loss and tiredness. Long-term complications can affect the eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart.
notes.tip: When asked to explain Type 1 and Type 2, compare them under four headings: cause, age of onset, treatment and whether it can be reversed. Diabetes is not caused by too much insulin: in Type 1 too little is made, and in Type 2 cells respond poorly.

notes.b: A diet low in fibre and fluid makes stools hard and dry, and the effort of passing them puts the large intestine under strain. Several bowel problems follow from this in a chain.
points: Constipation: hard, dry stools are passed with difficulty, usually caused by too little fibre and fluid and too little activity.
Diverticular disease: small pouches called diverticula form in the wall of the large intestine when the pressure from straining pushes the lining outwards.
Diverticulitis: inflamed or infected diverticula cause pain and need medical treatment.
Haemorrhoids: swollen veins around the anus, caused by straining during constipation.
A low-fibre diet also raises the risk of bowel disorders, including bowel cancer.

Prevention: eat wholegrain cereals, brown bread, wholegrain rice, pulses, nuts and seeds, and fruit and vegetables with their skins on, eaten raw where possible, because skins and raw plant foods keep most of their fibre.
Whole fruit and vegetables supply more fibre than juice, and fresh or dried fruit is a better snack than processed alternatives. Plenty of fluid, exercise and regular meals also help.
A high-fibre diet reduces the risk of bowel disease.
notes.tip: For a question on preventing bowel disease, give high-fibre foods with examples, plus plenty of fluid and exercise. In true or false questions, a high-fibre diet reducing the risk of bowel disease is true.

notes.b: Bones are living tissue that is built up in childhood and lost slowly in later life. Osteoporosis is a thinning and weakening of the bone, which becomes porous, brittle and prone to fracture.
points: Bone mass peaks in early adulthood, after which bone is gradually lost, so building strong bones in childhood and adolescence gives a bigger store to draw on later.
Too little calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C or phosphorus over life raises the risk. Vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium, and vitamin C is needed for the collagen framework of bone.
Phytates, oxalates, excess fibre and tannins in some foods can reduce calcium absorption, because they bind calcium in the gut.
Excess caffeine and alcohol increase calcium loss, and excess saturated fat can also reduce calcium availability.
Risk factors include older age, the fall in oestrogen after menopause (which puts women at higher risk), smoking and inactivity.
Weight-bearing exercise helps to maintain bone strength.

Prevention: increase calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C and phosphorus in the diet, build bone in childhood and adolescence, take weight-bearing exercise, and limit the inhibitors of calcium absorption listed above.
notes.tip: Meal planning guidelines for osteoporosis are asked at Higher Level: say to increase calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C and phosphorus, and to avoid inhibitors of calcium absorption such as phytates, oxalates, excess fibre, tannins, caffeine and alcohol. Do not confuse osteoporosis with rickets or osteomalacia, which are vitamin D deficiency diseases. Low calcium causing osteoporosis is a safe example of a cause.

notes.b: Teeth are damaged by acid made from sugar in the mouth. Dental caries (tooth decay) and gum disease are separate problems, although both start with plaque.
points: Bacteria in plaque ferment sugars in the mouth to produce acid, which dissolves enamel and causes dental caries.
Frequent snacking, sticky sweets and sugary drinks keep the mouth acidic for longer, which increases the risk of decay.
Fluoride strengthens enamel and makes it more resistant to acid; fluoride toothpaste is used twice a day.
Calcium, phosphorus and vitamin D support the formation of enamel and dentine, the teeth's hard tissues.
Periodontal (gum) disease is inflammation of the gums and the tissues around the teeth, caused by a build-up of plaque.
Protection: limit sugary food to mealtimes, brush, have dental check-ups, and eat cheese and crunchy fruit and vegetables.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two conditions: caries damages tooth enamel, while periodontal disease inflames the gums. Stick to obesity, caries and diabetes when discussing the effects of sugar.

notes.b: Diet problems rarely come singly. A surplus of one nutrient or too little of another can lead to several conditions, and some conditions lead on to others.
points: Excess energy leads to obesity, which increases the risk of Type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease and high blood pressure.
Excess salt raises blood pressure, which increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
A diet high in sugar contributes to both obesity and dental caries.
A low-fibre, low-fluid diet can cause constipation, which in turn can lead to diverticular disease.
Too little calcium and vitamin D leads to osteoporosis, and too little iron leads to anaemia.
A poor diet in a teenager can cause several problems at once: overweight, CHD risk, tooth decay, constipation, anaemia, diabetes risk and osteoporosis later.
notes.tip: Given a poor menu, name the condition and then explain how the menu causes it. The condition and the explanation are marked separately, so give both.

keyTerms.definition: A measure of weight for height, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.
A condition of excess body fat resulting from a sustained energy surplus, which raises the risk of other diseases.
Narrowing or blockage of the coronary arteries that supply the heart muscle with blood.
A hormone made by the pancreas that lowers blood glucose by moving it into body cells.
A condition in which the body's cells respond poorly to insulin, mainly linked to excess weight and inactivity.
Conditions in which small pouches form in the wall of the large intestine, often caused by straining on a low-fibre diet.
A thinning and weakening of bone that makes it porous, brittle and prone to fracture.
Decay of the teeth caused by acid produced when bacteria in plaque ferment sugars.
Inflammation and infection of the gums and the tissues that support the teeth.

factCards.definition: Coronary heart disease, Type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure.
The body's cells respond poorly to insulin; it is linked to excess weight and inactivity.

factCards.term: Four factors that raise the risk of osteoporosis
factCards.definition: Low calcium intake; inactivity; smoking; excess alcohol.

factCards.term: Two dietary ways to prevent constipation
factCards.definition: Eat high-fibre wholegrains, fruit and vegetables; drink plenty of water.

factCards.term: Three dietary guidelines to reduce dental caries
factCards.definition: Limit sugary snacks and drinks, especially between meals; choose water or milk to drink; use fluoride toothpaste.

factCards.term: Three effects of excess salt on the body
factCards.definition: It raises blood pressure, damages artery walls and increases the risk of stroke.

questions.prompt: Outline two diet-related problems that can result from a diet low in fibre and fluid.
questions.model: Constipation: without bulk and water, stools become hard and difficult to pass. Diverticular disease: straining to pass hard stools raises pressure in the large intestine and forms pouches in its wall. Haemorrhoids: swollen veins around the anus caused by straining during constipation. Any two problems, each named and explained, earn 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss the links between excess energy intake, obesity and two other diet-related conditions.
questions.model: Excess energy intake occurs when food energy regularly exceeds energy used, and the surplus is stored as adipose tissue, producing obesity, shown by a BMI of 30 or more. Obesity raises LDL cholesterol and blood pressure and narrows the coronary arteries, increasing the risk of coronary heart disease. Obesity also reduces insulin effectiveness, and excess sugar intake adds to the risk of Type 2 diabetes, where cells respond poorly to insulin. Obesity can also be linked to gallstones and high blood pressure. Dental caries is worsened by sugary foods eaten often, which produce acid in the mouth. Management: reduce energy and sugar intake, increase fibre and activity, and monitor weight.
